```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5, dpi = 96)
options(ecolongr.threads = 2)
```

This vignette follows one dataset from the file you download to an ordination.
The data is the 16S time series from the Linnaeus Microbial Observatory (LMO) in the Baltic Sea, 2011–2023, published through the [Swedish ASV portal](https://asv-portal.biodiversitydata.se/) and GBIF.
It was sampled about every two weeks, so the community should go round a seasonal cycle each year.
That is what we look for in the ordinations.

```{r libraries, message = FALSE}
library(duckplyr)
library(ecolongr)
```

## The data

The dataset is [`lmo_2011-2023_16s`](https://www.gbif.se/ipt/resource?r=lmo_2011-2023_16s) on the GBIF IPT of the Swedish node.
Its Darwin Core archive (109 MB zipped, 1.1 GB unpacked) holds 405,592 occurrences: one row per ASV and sample, with the read count in `organismQuantity`.
The same measurements table has the temperature and, for most samples, the salinity.
It has two size fractions of the water, stored as the measurement `filter_fraction` in `extendedmeasurementorfact.txt`: `3` (particle associated, trapped on a 3 µm filter) and `3-0.2` (free living, trapped on a 0.2 µm filter after the 3 µm one).

The archive has the layout of GBIF's standard Darwin Core archives, not that of the ZIP files the `asvoccur` package reads, so we read it directly.
`duckplyr` reads the tab-separated files without loading them into R, and the filtering stays lazy:

```{r download, eval = FALSE}
download.file("https://www.gbif.se/ipt/archive.do?r=lmo_2011-2023_16s", "lmo.zip", mode = "wb")
unzip("lmo.zip", exdir = "lmo")

tsv <- list(delim = "\t", quote = "", header = TRUE)
occurrence <- read_csv_duckdb("lmo/occurrence.txt", options = tsv, prudence = "stingy")

# all_varchar: the first rows of the measurements are numbers (temperature, salinity),
# which would make DuckDB read the whole column as numeric.
emof <- read_csv_duckdb("lmo/extendedmeasurementorfact.txt",
                        options = c(tsv, list(all_varchar = TRUE)), prudence = "stingy")

free_living <- emof |>
  filter(measurementType == "filter_fraction", measurementValue == "3-0.2") |>
  select(occurrenceID)

counts <- occurrence |>
  semi_join(free_living, by = "occurrenceID") |>
  transmute(sample = eventID, taxon = taxonID, quant = organismQuantity)

metadata <- occurrence |>
  semi_join(free_living, by = "occurrenceID") |>
  distinct(sample = eventID, date = eventDate, depth = minimumDepthInMeters) |>
  as.data.frame()
```

That is 162,171 rows, 347 samples and 24,286 ASVs.
`prudence = "stingy"` makes `duckplyr` stop with an error if it would otherwise copy a whole table into R.

To keep the vignette fast, the package contains a smaller version of the same table: the free-living fraction, with only the ASVs present in at least 5% of the samples (`data-raw/make_lmo_extdata.R` makes it from the archive, with the temperature and salinity of each sample).
The rest of the vignette uses it.

```{r bundled}
counts <- read_csv_duckdb(
  system.file("extdata", "lmo_free_living.tsv.gz", package = "ecolongr"),
  options = list(delim = "\t", header = TRUE), prudence = "stingy"
)
metadata <- read.delim(system.file("extdata", "lmo_free_living_samples.tsv", package = "ecolongr"))
metadata$date <- as.Date(metadata$date)
metadata$day_of_year <- as.integer(format(metadata$date, "%j"))
metadata$month <- factor(format(metadata$date, "%m"))

counts |> summarise(rows = n(), samples = n_distinct(sample), taxa = n_distinct(taxon)) |> as.data.frame()
```

## Filtering

The filters are `duckplyr` verbs, so the table is still not in R.
The depth of a sample is its number of reads in the table.

```{r depth}
depth <- counts |> summarise(reads = sum(quant, na.rm = TRUE), .by = sample)
summary(as.data.frame(depth)$reads)
```

We drop the samples with fewer than 5,000 reads, and later the ASVs that occur in fewer than 20% of the samples.
`duckplyr` does not translate `filter(sample %in% vector)` for a vector of this length, so we filter with a join, as in the README.
`el_vegdist()` and `el_rda()` can only see the samples that have rows, so we pass the sample table as `samples`: it sets the order of the results to the order of the metadata, which `adonis2()` and `envfit()` rely on.

```{r deep}
deep <- depth |> filter(reads >= 5000) |> select(sample)
counts <- counts |> semi_join(deep, by = "sample")

metadata <- metadata[metadata$sample %in% as.data.frame(deep)$sample, ]
nrow(metadata)
```

## Colouring by season

The axis labels of a PCA give the percentage of the total variance of the table that the axis holds: the eigenvalue divided by `tot.chi`, not by the sum of the kept eigenvalues.
We colour the samples by day of year, with a palette that returns to its start, so that a seasonal cycle shows as a ring with the colours in order.

```{r plot-helper}
season_colours <- function(day) hcl(h = 360 * day / 366, c = 90, l = 60)

plot_season <- function(ordination, main, ...) {
  sites <- vegan::scores(ordination, display = "sites", choices = 1:2)
  axes <- colnames(sites)
  if (inherits(ordination, "rda")) {
    percent <- 100 * vegan::eigenvals(ordination)[1:2] / ordination$tot.chi
    axes <- sprintf("%s (%.1f%%)", axes, percent)
  }
  plot(sites, col = season_colours(metadata$day_of_year), pch = 19, asp = 1, main = main,
       xlab = axes[1], ylab = axes[2], ...)
}
```

## Hellinger distances

Hellinger standardisation followed by Euclidean distance is a common choice for amplicon counts.
`el_decostand()` does the standardisation lazily, and `el_vegdist()` runs the query:

```{r hellinger}
d_hellinger <- counts |>
  el_decostand("hellinger") |>
  el_vegdist("euclidean", samples = metadata$sample)
class(d_hellinger)
attr(d_hellinger, "Size")
```

The result is a `dist`, so `vegan` takes over:

```{r adonis}
set.seed(1)
vegan::adonis2(d_hellinger ~ month, data = metadata, permutations = 199)
```

## Bray–Curtis distances and NMDS

Non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) uses only the ranks of the distances, so it needs no elaborate transformation.
A common choice is Bray–Curtis distance on relative abundances.
`el_decostand("total")` makes the relative abundances, and `vegan::metaMDS()` takes the `dist`.
Given a `dist`, `metaMDS()` has no species scores and does no transformation of its own, which it would do for a community matrix; that matrix is what this package avoids building.

```{r nmds}
d_bray <- counts |>
  el_decostand("total") |>
  el_vegdist("bray", samples = metadata$sample)

set.seed(1)
nmds <- vegan::metaMDS(d_bray, k = 2, trace = 0, trymax = 10)
nmds$stress
plot_season(nmds, "NMDS, Bray-Curtis on relative abundances")
```

The seasons are ordered along the cloud, but a few samples lie far from the rest and compress the view.

## Principal components

`el_rda()` computes the first axes of a PCA without making the dense table.

```{r pca-hellinger}
pca_hellinger <- counts |>
  el_decostand("hellinger") |>
  el_rda(k = 5, samples = metadata$sample)

plot_season(pca_hellinger, "Hellinger")
summary(pca_hellinger)$cont$importance[2:3, 1:3]
```

The colours follow each other around a ring, one lap per year, so the seasonal cycle is the main structure in the first two axes.

## The centred log-ratio

The Aitchison distance is the Euclidean distance on the centred log-ratio (clr) of the counts.
Zeros need a pseudocount.
A pseudocount of `1 / (the sample's reads)` in each sample lets a shallow sample, with its higher detection limit, get a larger pseudocount.
Give the raw counts: the pseudocount is in count units.
`pseudocount = "inverse_depth"` takes the reads from the table it is given, so we compute the depths from the whole table first and pass them by name, because we filter the ASVs below.

`clr` makes every cell non-zero, so it is not a method of `el_decostand()`.
It is computed from the counts inside the two functions that use it, and the dense table is never built.
`el_vegdist(method = "aitchison")` returns the Aitchison distance, and `el_rda(transform = "clr")` is a PCA of the clr, whose sample distances in all axes are the same Aitchison distances.

On amplicon data, the many rare ASVs dominate a clr unless they are removed.
We keep the ASVs present in at least 20% of the samples:

```{r clr-filter}
n_samples <- nrow(metadata)

depth <- counts |>
  summarise(total = sum(quant, na.rm = TRUE), .by = sample) |>
  as.data.frame()
pseudocount <- setNames(1 / depth$total, depth$sample)

common <- counts |>
  summarise(prevalence = n_distinct(sample), .by = taxon) |>
  filter(prevalence >= 0.2 * n_samples) |>
  select(taxon)

common |> summarise(taxa = n()) |> as.data.frame()

counts_common <- counts |> semi_join(common, by = "taxon")
```

```{r clr}
d_aitchison <- counts_common |>
  el_vegdist("aitchison", pseudocount = pseudocount, samples = metadata$sample)

pca_clr <- counts_common |>
  el_rda(k = 5, transform = "clr", pseudocount = pseudocount, samples = metadata$sample)

plot_season(pca_clr, "clr, ASVs in at least 20% of the samples")
summary(pca_clr)$cont$importance[2:3, 1:3]
```

The cycle is there as well, as a filled disc rather than a thin ring.

For comparison, the same PCA with all the ASVs of the bundled table (those in at least 5% of the samples):

```{r clr-all}
pca_clr_all <- counts |>
  el_rda(k = 5, transform = "clr", pseudocount = pseudocount, samples = metadata$sample)

plot_season(pca_clr_all, "clr, ASVs in at least 5% of the samples")
```

With the ASVs that occur in 5–20% of the samples included, the points spread out more and the order of the colours is less clear.

## Environmental variables

The temperature and the salinity of each sample are in `metadata`.
`vegan::envfit()` fits them to the ordination, as arrows in the plot, and gives the share of variation each explains and a permutation p-value.
Samples without a salinity are dropped with `na.rm = TRUE`.

```{r envfit}
env <- metadata[, c("temperature", "salinity")]

set.seed(3)
fit <- vegan::envfit(pca_clr, env, choices = 1:2, permutations = 199, na.rm = TRUE)
fit

plot_season(pca_clr, "clr, with temperature and salinity", xlim = c(-8, 12))
plot(fit, add = TRUE, arrow.mul = 5)
```

Temperature lies along the first axis and explains much more of the variation (`r2`) than salinity, which points the other way.

## Filling the zeros: `rclr`

The robust clr (`rclr`) takes the logarithm of the non-zero counts only and fills the zeros by a low-rank matrix completion.
`vegan::decostand(x, "rclr")` does this, and so do `el_vegdist(method = "robust.aitchison")` and `el_rda(transform = "rclr")`, on the raw counts and without the dense table.
Every cell is filled, so `el_decostand("rclr")` cannot return it as a table without zeros; it only takes the log-ratio of the non-zero cells.

The completion has rank `ropt`, 3 as in `vegan`, so a PCA of it has at most `ropt` axes:

```{r rclr}
pca_rclr <- counts |>
  el_rda(k = 3, transform = "rclr", ropt = 3, samples = metadata$sample)

plot_season(pca_rclr, "rclr, completion of rank 3")
summary(pca_rclr)$cont$importance[2:3, ]
```

The three axes hold all the variance of the completed matrix by construction.
To get more axes, raise `ropt`: the cost of the completion grows with the rank, and only rank 3 has been timed on large tables.

## How much do the axes leave out?

`el_rda()` keeps the first `k` axes.
The total variance of the table is still known, so the share that the other axes hold can be computed:

```{r unexplained}
unexplained <- function(pca) 1 - sum(vegan::eigenvals(pca)) / pca$tot.chi
round(c(hellinger = unexplained(pca_hellinger), clr = unexplained(pca_clr)), 2)
```

The share of an axis is its eigenvalue divided by the total variance, `tot.chi`, which `summary()` does.
Dividing by the sum of the kept eigenvalues is wrong.
Those shares sum to one over the `k` axes whatever `k` is, so they hide what the other axes hold:

```{r share-right-wrong}
eig <- vegan::eigenvals(pca_clr)
round(rbind(
  right = eig / pca_clr$tot.chi,
  wrong = eig / sum(eig)
), 3)
```

## Seasonal structure in the distances

A distance matrix is what `vegan::adonis2()` needs.
The month explains this share of the variation in each distance:

```{r adonis-both}
set.seed(2)
r2 <- sapply(
  list(hellinger = d_hellinger, aitchison = d_aitchison),
  function(d) vegan::adonis2(d ~ month, data = metadata, permutations = 99)$R2[1]
)
round(r2, 2)
```

## Memory

Nothing above held the table as a dense matrix.
For the full table the distance matrix is the largest object (one number per pair of samples), and the rest of the work is done in batches.
See the README for settings and measurements on much larger tables.
